title: How is a hurricane born? 🌀
hook: How is a hurricane born, a storm that can spin over half a country?

scenes.narration: How is a hurricane born, a storm that can spin over half a country?
It all starts over a very warm sea, above twenty-six degrees Celsius.
Warm, moist air rises, cools and builds huge clouds, which release even more heat.
Below, it leaves a low-pressure zone that sucks in the air around it.
And since the Earth rotates, that air doesn't flow straight in: it curves, and the whole thing starts to spin.
At the center is the eye, a calm zone, surrounded by the most violent wall of the storm.
scenes.on_screen_text: The eye: calm at the center

scenes.narration: In the strongest ones, the wind tops two hundred and fifty kilometers per hour.
When it reaches land it loses its fuel, the warm water, and slowly weakens.
And they almost never form near the equator, because there Earth's spin can't get them rotating. That's why Ecuador doesn't get hurricanes.
Send this to someone who lives where hurricanes hit.
scenes.on_screen_text: Send this to someone in their path

description: Hurricanes are born over seas warmer than about 26 °C: warm, moist air rises, builds clouds that release heat, and leaves a low-pressure zone below that pulls in more air. Earth's rotation makes that air spin, with a calm eye at the center. At category 5 winds top 252 km/h. They weaken over land, and they almost never form near the equator. Original 3D animation.

claims.statement: Tropical cyclones need ocean water of at least about 26.5 °C.
The Coriolis force makes hurricanes spin: counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern.
A category 5 hurricane has sustained winds of 252 km/h or more.
Tropical cyclones almost never form within about 5° of the equator, where the Coriolis effect is minimal.
